hints: Focus on how much catalyst is present at the very start, when almost no product has formed yet.
Notice that as a little product forms, the reaction speeds itself up, so the rate must first rise from zero.
Consider what must happen later when reactants start to run out, even though lots of catalyst is now present.
walkthrough:
**Think about the start**

At time = 0, there is no product yet, so there is no catalyst yet. That means the initial rate must be zero or very close to zero.

$$\text{rate at } t=0 \approx 0$$

**Think about the middle**

As the reaction slowly proceeds, a little product forms. This product acts as a catalyst, so it speeds the reaction up. More product means more catalyst, so the rate increases sharply.

$$\text{product formed} \rightarrow \text{more catalyst} \rightarrow \text{faster rate}$$

**Think about the end**

Later, even though there is plenty of catalyst, the concentration of reactants has fallen a lot. With fewer reactant particles to collide, the rate must fall again toward zero. A rise then a fall gives a peaked curve starting at the origin.

options.A: This starts with a high rate that levels off and stays high. That cannot be autocatalysis because the rate starts at zero when no catalyst exists, and it must fall at the end when reactants are used up, not stay constant.
options.B: This starts slowly then levels off at a high constant rate. This S-shape is a common trap because it looks like the concentration-time curve for the product, not the rate-time curve. Rate must decrease at the end as reactants run out.
options.C: This is correct. Rate starts at zero, rises to a maximum as autocatalyst builds up, then falls as reactant concentration becomes the limiting factor. This rise-and-fall peaked shape is characteristic of autocatalysis.
options.D: This shows maximum rate at time = 0 followed by a continuous fall. That is the normal curve for an ordinary reaction where reactants are highest at the start. It ignores the slow start caused by having no catalyst initially.
